text: Why does two's complement make a subtractor unnecessary?
choices: Because a - b equals a + (-b) in arithmetic modulo 2^n, and negation is invert-and-add-one, so one adder does both operations.
Because subtraction of two's complement numbers never overflows, so no separate circuit is needed.
Because the sign bit lets the adder detect which operation was intended and switch modes.
Because subtraction is performed by the compiler at build time whenever possible.
explanation: This is the reason the representation was chosen, and it is a good example of a design decision paying off in silicon rather than in elegance. Sign-magnitude needs a comparator, a subtractor, and logic to decide the result's sign. Two's complement needs an inverter and the adder you already had — which is a real reduction in transistor count, and it is why every processor you will use represents integers this way.
